quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn's death on 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County is documented in the tree by S3 (Pennsylvania Death Certificates), which is cited both on his death fact and on the parent-child relationship with Thomas Flynn. However, no parentage assertions have been extracted from this record for q_001. The Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906-1968 collection is name-searchable. Pennsylvania death certificates from 1906 required the informant to supply both parents' names; reading the parents fields on this certificate is the highest-probability single step and may directly name Thomas as father and reveal the mother's name. Variant spellings Flynn and Flinn should both be checked.

The 1860 census (S2 in the tree) is already cited on the Thomas-Patrick parent-child relationship but no assertions from it have been extracted for q_001. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818, Ireland) would be ~42 and Patrick (~1845) would be ~15 in 1860. Though the 1860 census does not state relationships, finding both in the same household adds further indirect parentage evidence; the same household may also show Thomas's wife, whose name would begin to identify the mother. The United States Census, 1860 collection is name-searchable. Variants: Flynn and Flinn.

Thomas Flynn (~1818) would be ~52 and Patrick (~1845) would be ~25 in 1870. Patrick may by now head his own household nearby; either way, the 1870 census may show Thomas's wife alongside him, beginning to identify the mother. If Patrick heads his own household, his neighbors and nearby households may reveal relatives. The United States Census, 1870 collection is name-searchable. Variants: Flynn and Flinn.

Ancestry's independent 1870 United States Federal Census index uses different transcription than FamilySearch and can recover entries missed when searching by variant spellings. If pli_006 fails to locate Thomas or Patrick Flynn, search here at https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7163/ with both Flynn and Flinn variants.

The 1880 census is the first to state each person's relationship to the head of household and each person's father's and mother's birthplace. If Patrick Flynn (~35 in 1880) appears in Thomas Flynn's household with 'Son' in the relationship column, that is a direct statement of parentage. If Patrick heads his own household by 1880, his parents' birthplace columns corroborate the Ireland origin. Thomas Flynn (~62 in 1880) may appear with his wife, further identifying the mother. The United States Census, 1880 collection is name-searchable.

Patrick Flynn (~55 in 1900) likely heads his own household and the 1900 census states each person's father's birthplace and mother's birthplace, as well as month and year of birth confirming the ca. 1845 estimate. If Thomas Flynn survived to ~82, he could appear in Patrick's or a sibling's household. The United States Census, 1900 collection is name-searchable.

Schuylkill County probate records (wills, administrations) are held at the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 (loc_001). Thomas Flynn (born ~1818, Ireland) could plausibly have died between 1860 and 1900; this date range is bounded by Thomas's plausible lifespan, not Patrick's research window. A will naming Patrick Flynn as a son would be direct evidence of parentage; an intestate administration naming all heirs carries equal force. The Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994 collection is browse-only (personCount 0) — this is an image browse of the county docket index, not a name search. The docket index must be browsed year by year for Schuylkill County; some county probate films in the anthracite region are browse-only image groups (loc_001 quirk).

A dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to his wife is required for this parentage question. This record names both parties, establishing the mother's surname and given name before she appears in any census. loc_001 lists two name-searchable marriage collections covering this period on FamilySearch: Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900 and Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677-1950. Thomas Flynn (~1818) married before Patrick's birth (~1845 in Ireland), suggesting a marriage circa 1835-1845; a Pennsylvania marriage in the late 1840s after immigration is also possible. If the marriage occurred in Ireland before the family emigrated, it may not appear in Pennsylvania records — an Irish parish church search would then follow as a later step. Variant: Flynn and Flinn for Thomas.

As Irish immigrants in Schuylkill County's anthracite coal region, the Flynn family was likely Roman Catholic; parishes here fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1875, when parts of the region shifted to the Diocese of Scranton (loc_001). The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable and spans 1708-1985. A search targets: (a) Patrick Flynn's confirmation record (~1858-1862), which often names sponsors who could be relatives and corroborate the family; (b) baptism entries for Patrick's siblings, which name both parents and identify the mother; (c) any Thomas Flynn or wife marriage entry recorded after immigration. Note: some church films for this region are browse-only image groups (loc_001 quirk); if the specific parish is identified, a targeted image browse may be needed alongside the name search.

Patrick Flynn was born ~1845 in Ireland and would have been 16-20 years old during the Civil War (1861-1865), squarely within service age for Pennsylvania volunteer regiments. Military service records and pension applications routinely documented a soldier's birthplace, parents' names, and sometimes the full family. A Civil War pension file is a detailed record that can name parents, childhood residence, and siblings — all direct evidence for this parentage question. The United States, Civil War Soldiers Index, 1861-1865 collection is name-searchable. If Patrick appears there, his compiled service record and pension file would be the follow-on searches at NARA or on Fold3. Variants: Flynn and Flinn.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree holds the couple and five children; no records have been searched yet for any others.

entry.rationale: The 1850 federal census (United States Census, 1850, collection 1401638 per loc_001, name-searchable) names every household member with age and birthplace. Thomas Hale would be head of household; all children at home in 1850 would appear. The five known children span births ~1836–1847, so all should be listed here, alongside any additional child born before 1850 who was still at home.

The 1860 federal census (United States Census, 1860, collection 1473181 per loc_001, name-searchable) names every household member. Thomas was alive and would be head of household. Any child born between 1848 and 1860 — the decade after the youngest known child Joseph (b. ~1847) — would appear here and would not have been captured in the 1850 census.

Thomas died in 1868. His estate — whether testate or intestate — would have been administered through the Greene County Probate Court (held probate jurisdiction after 1852, per loc_001 quirks). A will naming children is direct evidence of parentage and of the full sibling set; intestate proceedings list all legal heirs. Ohio Probate Records, 1789-1996 (collection 1992421 per loc_001, name-searchable) covers this period. The date range extends to 1885 to allow for multi-year administration or ancillary proceedings. Sarah's probate, whenever she died, should also be searched during the same run.

Children of Thomas and Sarah who married in Greene County would appear in Ohio County Marriages, 1789-2016 (collection 1614804 per loc_001, name-searchable). Marriage records in this era sometimes name the bride's or groom's parents. Searching all Hale marriages in Greene County during the period when the children would have been of marrying age (~1854–1900) may surface additional children not found in census records. The date range opens at 1854 when Mary (b. ~1836) reaches marriageable age.

Thomas died in 1868. The 1870 census (United States Census, 1870, collection 1438024 per loc_001, name-searchable) would show Sarah Hale as head of household — or residing with an adult child — along with any children still at home. Children born ~1860–1868 would be 2–10 years old in 1870 and would not have appeared in prior census households. Older children who established separate households in Greene County would also be traceable here.

The 1840 federal census lists only the head of household by name, with other members tallied in age-and-sex columns. Thomas Hale would be head; Mary (b. ~1836) would appear as a female aged 0–4. Comparing the number of children in each age-and-sex column against the five known children may reveal an older child born ~1832–1835 who does not appear in the 1850 household, or a child who died before 1850 and left no other record.

The 1880 census explicitly records each person's relationship to the head of household — the most useful relationship column of any pre-1900 census. Twelve years after Thomas's death, Sarah (if living) or adult children may be found in Greene County. Any child born ~1860–1868 would be 12–20 and likely in a family household; older children would be in their own nearby households. Searching all Hale households in Greene County and reviewing ages, relationships and birthplaces will extend and cross-check the sibling group.

Ohio civil birth registration did not begin until 1867. Church baptism and christening registers are the primary source for children's births in this era. FamilySearch holds some Ohio church records; a search spanning 1832–1867 covers the full plausible birth window for Thomas (b. ~1810) and Sarah's children. Children who died in infancy and never appeared in a named census household are especially likely to be found only in a baptism register.

Ohio began death registration in 1867. Thomas Hale's 1868 death certificate — if one was filed — would name his wife and potentially surviving children. Death certificates for the five known children, when they eventually died, would name their parents and sometimes list surviving siblings. Searching for death records of the Hale surname in Greene County across this range may surface an additional child whose death certificate names Thomas and Sarah as parents. The date range extends to 1920 to allow for long-lived children born in the 1850s or 1860s.

FAN-cluster item: land deeds and tax records name witnesses, grantors and boundary neighbors — often relatives. When Thomas sold or mortgaged property, or when his estate disposed of real estate after his 1868 death, children would be named as grantors or heirs. Adjoining landowners named in deed boundary recitals are neighbors and potential relatives. Searching land records for Thomas's entire Greene County residence (~1830s to 1868) and the immediate post-death period may name children who had already left the household before the 1850 census snapshot.

Civil birth registration for Ohio children born before 1867 — including all likely children of Thomas and Sarah — did not exist. Church baptism records (item 8) are the substitute source for this period.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Finding him completes coverage of the high-severity 1860–1908 timeline gap alongside pli_011 and pli_012, ensuring the subject is tracked through his adult life. Schuylkill County Naturalization Records 1849–1915 (image group 007936750) are browse-only (personCount 0). Thomas Flynn, born ~1818 in Ireland, would have naturalized in Schuylkill County. This plan is for the question of who Patrick Flynn's parents were — specifically, it now turns away from the census and death certificate sources that have already been searched and looks instead at the records of Thomas Flynn himself and Patrick's wider circle. Together these ten searches draw on census records, probate, church, vital, naturalization, and land records — six distinct record types covering Thomas's documents, Patrick's later life, and the neighborhood network around both men.

The next step is to begin executing the plan, starting with the name-searchable 1880 federal census search targeting Thomas Flynn's household in Schuylkill County.

Finding Michael already in Schuylkill in 1880 revises the "around 1882" date; finding him still elsewhere narrows the relocation window. His occupation column tests whether the shift from farming to mining was immediate on arrival.

- **pli_003** — census, Schuylkill County, 1880, FamilySearch (US Census 1880, FAN search for Patrick Sheahan): Patrick holds a Schuylkill County deed from 1875 (S1). This search finds Patrick's 1880 household, confirms his occupation, and reveals whether he was employed as a miner and whether other Sheahans were already with him — directly testing the chain-migration hypothesis.

- **pli_004** — census, Schuylkill County, 1900, FamilySearch (US Census 1900): The 1900 schedule uniquely records "year of immigration" and "years in the United States," placing Michael's US arrival date independently and corroborating or refining the "around 1882" estimate. Occupation column tests whether coal employment was sustained.

- **pli_005** — church, Schuylkill County, 1875–1895, FamilySearch (Schuylkill County Church Records, 982,415 persons): A sacramental entry — marriage, child's baptism, or appearance as witness — in a Schuylkill County Catholic parish would narrow Michael's arrival date to before that event. Parishes were under the Diocese of Philadelphia/Scranton.

- **pli_006** — immigration/naturalization, Schuylkill County, 1849–1915, FamilySearch (browse-only, image group 007936750, ~298 images): Naturalization petitions record the petitioner's US arrival date and may name their employer or mining ward. Patrick Sheahan's papers, if present, provide chain-migration context. Browse required — 0% indexed.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

The church records browse volume 007936751 (1842-1895, browse-only) is an additional fallback for parishes not in the indexed collection.

Since Patrick was born in Ireland (~1845), his baptism does not appear in Schuylkill County records — this burial record item fulfills the Step 3 requirement for a subject whose baptism cannot exist in the searched jurisdiction. The state death certificate (1908, pli_005, completed) was already found and names Thomas Flynn as father, but its informant (son-in-law James Brown) is secondary and recorded the birthplace as Pennsylvania in error. A Catholic parish burial register entry is an independent original source recorded by the priest, often from family members present at the death — typically more accurate for origin detail. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985) is name-searchable (personCount above 0); search for Patrick Flynn death or burial entries around 1908. A burial entry naming Ireland as birthplace would corroborate the census evidence against the death certificate's Pennsylvania error, and any parentage information recorded there is an independent secondary source.

Patrick Flynn was born ~1845 and would have been 16-20 during the Civil War (1861-1865) — within service age for Pennsylvania volunteers. The United States, Civil War Soldiers Index, 1861-1865 (collection 1910717) is name-searchable (personCount above 0); a positive hit would point to a service record and potentially a pension file. Civil War pension files regularly contain family affidavits, declarations of dependency, and marriage certificates that name parents, wives, and children — a contextual record type (BCG Standard 12) with meaningful secondary parentage value. Even a negative result narrows the picture. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.question: Where did Josiah Rowe (b. ~1828, Ohio) reside between 1850 and 1865, and with whom was he living?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree places Josiah in Vigo County, Indiana at his death in 1879 and gives Ohio as his birthplace, but nothing is documented between his birth and his 1862 enlistment. No records have been searched yet.

entry.rationale: Josiah (b. ~1828 Ohio) was ~22 in 1850 and may still have been in his parents' household or had struck out on his own. The 1850 federal census names every household member but does not state relationships between them (loc_001 quirk). Loc_001 lists collection 1401638 for this census. Search nationally under Rowe, Row, and Roe because his destination state is unknown at this date. A match directly establishes both his 1850 residence and the names of co-residents — the two answers the question requires.

Fallback for pli_001 if FamilySearch's indexing does not surface Josiah. Ancestry's separate index for the 1850 census (U.S. Federal Census collection) may carry different spelling-variant coverage or capture a name the FamilySearch index missed. Try Rowe, Row, and Roe with no state filter first, then narrow to Ohio and Indiana.

By 1860 Josiah was ~32; he enlisted in Indiana in 1862 (tree fact), so he was likely in Indiana by 1860. The 1860 census names every household member without stating relationships (loc_001 quirk). Loc_001 lists collection 1473181 for this census. A match would show his residence and household composition immediately before his Civil War enlistment, completing coverage of the last full census year inside the question's window.

Fallback for pli_003 if FamilySearch does not surface Josiah in 1860. Ancestry's index for the 1860 census may catch spelling variants or indexing differences. Try Rowe, Row, and Roe with Indiana and neighboring states as filters.

The tree records Josiah's military service 1862-1865 in Indiana with no source attached. Indiana Civil War service records typically state the county and township of enlistment and may note next of kin or occupation. Finding his enlistment record anchors his Indiana residence in 1862 and may identify the household he left behind.

Fallback for pli_005 if FamilySearch does not hold the relevant Indiana regimental records. Fold3 holds NARA Compiled Military Service Records (federal-level), which often contain more physical description detail and unit history than state muster rolls and may carry an enlistment-residence notation.

Loc_001 lists 'United States Civil War and Later Pension Files, 1861-1934' (collection 1888129). A pension file — if Josiah or a dependent applied — routinely names the soldier's wife, children, and residence at the time of application, with neighbor depositions that speak to household composition during the question's window. Josiah died in 1879, so a widow's pension could also exist post-1879. Date range is sized to the collection (which runs past the question's 1865 endpoint) because pension depositions testify to events inside the 1850-1865 window and an item capped at 1865 would miss the file entirely.

Loc_001 quirk: Indiana probate and marriage records exist for Vigo County but are not indexed in a surfaced collection; they must be searched through the county clerk and the Master Commissioner. If Josiah married before 1865, the marriage bond or license would name his spouse (a household co-resident) and often names a bondsman who was a relative, adding a second family member to the picture. The marriage date anchors when his household changed from family-of-origin to family-of-procreation.

Annual tax lists for Vigo County would show when Josiah first appears as a taxable resident, narrowing his arrival date from Ohio. Township notation pinpoints his neighborhood within the county. Consecutive-year presence confirms continuous residence and fills the inter-census gaps (1851-1859 and 1861-1862) where no enumeration record exists. Loc_001 did not surface a named, indexed collection for Vigo County tax records; this may be an image-browse search or require referral to the county if no FamilySearch volumes are found.

FAN item targeting household identification. Because the 1850 and 1860 censuses do not state relationships between household members (loc_001 quirk), the probate or estate records of Rowe co-residents found in those censuses are needed to confirm who they were relative to Josiah. If he was living with his parents in 1850, a father's will or estate filed after his death may name Josiah as a beneficiary, confirming a filial tie. Date range is sized to the death window of likely co-residents: persons aged 20-60 in 1850 would plausibly die 1865-1900. Loc_001 quirk: these records are accessed through the county clerk and Master Commissioner, not through a FamilySearch indexed collection. This item directly answers the 'with whom was he living' part of the question by establishing the relationship of named co-residents to Josiah.

- pli_003 · census · United States · FamilySearch · seq 3 — 1860 federal census; Josiah at ~32, likely Indiana given 1862 enlistment; shows household composition just before military service
- pli_004 · census · United States · Ancestry · seq 4 · fallback for pli_003 — same 1860 census on Ancestry as alternate index
- pli_005 · military · Indiana, United States · FamilySearch · seq 5 — Indiana Civil War service records; enlistment record states county/township of enlistment and may name next of kin, anchoring Indiana residence in 1862
- pli_006 · military · Indiana, United States · Fold3 · seq 6 · fallback for pli_005 — NARA Compiled Military Service Records; federal-level records with more physical detail than state muster rolls
